title: The note inside.
teaser: Little follows a tiny tap into a room full of sound.
question: Where does a piano's note come from?
idea: In an acoustic piano, pressing a key moves a mechanism that sends a felt-covered hammer against strings. The strings vibrate. A wooden bridge carries their motion to the soundboard, which moves more air so we can hear the note well.

curiosity.intro: Choose a question with your grown-up. Look for a clue in the picture before you open the explanation.
curiosity.carryForward: Follow Little's note through the story. Then compare two drawn lengths and keep a discovery in your own words.

questions.question: Where could a note be hiding?
questions.notice: Find Little's hand and the orange arrow. One key moves only a little. Where would you look for what happens next?
questions.say: The piano is not a box of stored notes. Pressing a key starts moving parts inside. In an acoustic piano, those parts send a small hammer toward metal strings. The next picture lets us look at a model of that hidden motion.
questions.try: Pretend the tabletop is a piano key. Lower one finger quietly, then lift it. Tell your grown-up what you imagine moving inside.

questions.question: How can a string keep singing after one tap?
questions.notice: Find the gap between the hammer and the string. Look for the two faint orange traces. What might they help us imagine?
questions.say: A hammer taps the string and falls away. The string keeps moving back and forth very quickly. That motion is vibration. The orange traces exaggerate the movement; they are not extra strings. The vibration gradually fades unless something stops it sooner.
questions.try: Move one finger a tiny distance back and forth in the air. Let it become still. Say when your pretend string could make sound.

questions.question: How does a thin string fill a room with sound?
questions.notice: Find the narrow raised bridge and the broad wooden board. Where do the strings meet the bridge? Follow the orange mark into the wood.
questions.say: A thin string alone moves little air. Its vibration passes through the bridge into the soundboard. This broad wooden board vibrates too, moving more air. The moving air carries sound to our ears. The wood helps us hear a small string's motion.
questions.try: Trace the path with your finger: string, bridge, soundboard. Finish by pointing toward your ear. What helped the motion reach you?

questions.question: Why do the two ends of a piano sound different?
questions.notice: The display has two strings. Trace each from one support to the other. What is different about the distance between the supports?
questions.say: Pitch means how high or low a note sounds. With other things the same, a longer string gives a lower pitch and a shorter one gives a higher pitch. Tightening the same string raises its pitch; loosening it lowers the pitch. In a piano, length, thickness, and tension work together. Low notes are toward the player's left; high notes are toward the right.
questions.try: Use your voice to make a comfortable low hum, then a higher hum. Keep both gentle. Can a high sound be quiet too?

plates.title: One small press
plates.alt: Little Wonderer sits at a walnut grand piano and presses a white key beneath a small orange arrow. Big stands close beside the bench in a sunlit music museum.
plates.caption: A tiny movement begins a question. This imagined museum piano is an acoustic piano, with strings inside.

plates.title: A hidden tap
plates.alt: Big and Little study an enlarged wooden key-action model. A long key tilts on a pivot; connected parts lift a felt hammer toward a horizontal string above it.
plates.caption: An enlarged, simplified grand-piano action. The key starts linked parts moving; the hammer taps and comes away.

plates.title: After the tap
plates.alt: A taut string spans two fixed supports on a museum table. A felt hammer sits below it with a clear gap. Faint orange traces show back-and-forth motion as Big and Little watch.
plates.caption: One string, shown with exaggerated motion traces. Real piano-string vibrations are much smaller and faster than this drawing can show.

plates.title: The wood joins in
plates.alt: The pair look at a broad pale wooden soundboard in a cutaway display. Strings meet a raised wooden bridge; an orange mark continues from the bridge into the board.
plates.caption: The bridge carries vibration into the soundboard. This cutaway leaves out parts so we can notice the connection.

plates.title: Two lengths to notice
plates.alt: Big and Little examine two separate taut strings on a wooden display. Orange brackets labeled longer and shorter follow the distance between each string's supports.
plates.caption: A comparison model, not two measured piano strings. Compare length while imagining the material, thickness, and tension stay the same.

plates.title: Keep the path
plates.alt: Big and Little share a notebook near the quiet piano. Little holds a pencil above sketches of a key, a hammer, strings, and a wooden board joined by orange arrows.
plates.caption: Little's sketch keeps a path through the piano. What small connection could you add?

reading.title: The note inside
reading.coverText: One key moves. A note rings out. Little follows it inside.
reading.parentNote: About 15 min: share the six short scenes, then revisit a picture. Read aloud for Leo; pointing, talking, and pausing count. Let Little's first guess hang in the air before following the clues. The foldable carries the same story.

beats.title: One small press
beats.passage: One key sinks beneath Little's hand. A note rings through the museum. “Was it hiding in there?” Little asks. Big listens beside the bench. The key hardly moved. Something inside the piano must have done much more.
beats.prompt: What would you look for inside? Keep your guess for the next picture.

beats.title: A hidden tap
beats.passage: An enormous model gives them a peek. A key tips; connected parts lift a felt-covered hammer. Tap! The hammer strikes a string and comes away. “A tiny hammer?” Little whispers. This team of moving parts is called the action.
beats.prompt: Follow the model from key to hammer. Why might the hammer need to come away?

beats.title: After the tap
beats.passage: The hammer has fallen back, but the string is not still. It quivers: back and forth, back and forth. That quick motion is vibration. “The tap is over,” Little says, “but the moving isn't!” How can such a thin string sound so big?
beats.prompt: Find the gap. What keeps moving after the hammer's tap?

beats.title: The wood joins in
beats.passage: Little follows a string to a wooden bridge. The bridge carries vibration into a broad soundboard. That wood vibrates too, moving more air. The air carries sound to listening ears. “The wood joins in!” Little says. A thin string has a roomy helper.
beats.prompt: Trace the connection into the wood. What does the soundboard help move?

beats.title: Two lengths to notice
beats.passage: Two strings stretch across another model. One is longer. If everything else stays the same, the longer string vibrates more slowly and sounds lower. The shorter one sounds higher. “Different voices!” says Little. How high or low a note sounds is its pitch.
beats.prompt: Point to the string you predict would sound lower. What must stay the same for this comparison?

beats.title: Keep the path
beats.passage: With the pedal up, Little releases a middle key. A felt damper hushes its strings. Little sketches key, hammer, strings, wood. “The note wasn't hiding. We set things moving!” Big leaves room for one more why.
beats.prompt: What changed Little's first guess? What connection could you add to the sketch?

words.meaning: the connected moving parts that send a piano hammer toward its strings
how high or low a sound seems to our ears
the pulling force that keeps a string stretched tight

questions: What did Little first guess about the note? Which moving parts helped change that guess?
How does vibration get from a string to the air? Name the two wooden helpers.

math.title: Longer by how much?
math.intro: Little wants two string lines for a drawing. Imagine line A is 24 centimeters long and line B is 9 centimeters long. Use the pretend lengths in the table.
math.printNote: These are invented drawing lengths. Do not measure the painting or real piano strings.

tasks.label: FIND THE DIFFERENCE
tasks.prompt: Line A is 24 cm long. Line B is 9 cm long. How much longer is A?
tasks.hint: Hop from 9 to 10, then to 20, then to 24. Add your hops.

tasks.label: JOIN THE LENGTHS
tasks.prompt: Imagine drawing A and B end to end. What is their total length?
tasks.hint: Add 6 to reach 30. How much of the 9 is left?

tasks.label: SHORTEN A DRAWING
tasks.prompt: Little erases 6 cm from line A. How long is that line now?
tasks.hint: Take away 4 to reach 20, then take away 2 more.

math.extension: Sketch two bars that start at the same place. Show which part is the extra 15 cm. A sketch need not be actual size.
math.parentNote: About 15 min: 3 to read the table, 9 to sketch or calculate, 3 to explain. A centimeter is a unit of length; cm is its short name. Use number-line hops or bar sketches, and accept a spoken strategy. The table supplies all numbers. These lengths do not predict exact piano notes. No instrument or measuring tools are needed.

writing.title: Give the note a path.
writing.intro: Choose one picture from Little's search. Tell what moves and what happens next. Draw or write a clue that helped you understand the note.
writing.draw: Draw one detail from your scene. Add an arrow or a label to show a movement or a difference.

frames.hint: What does the action help the hammer do?
How does the broad wood help move air?

frames.start: If only the string's length changes,
frames.hint: Which length could make the lower sound?

writing.check: Read it together and point to the detail your words explain. If you are writing, check the first capital and the ending mark.
writing.parentNote: About 15 min: 3 to choose and talk, 4 to draw, 6 for 1–3 sentences, 2 to read back. One careful idea is enough. Welcome speech, dictation, invented spelling, or a labeled drawing. Write Leo's words as he says them, then read them back together.

answers.label: Math · 1
answers.text: 15 cm longer: 24 − 9 = 15. Counting up from 9 in hops of 1, 10, and 4 is one strategy.

answers.label: Math · 2
answers.text: 33 cm in all: 24 + 9 = 33. Split 9 into 6 and 3 to bridge through 30.

answers.label: Math · 3
answers.text: 18 cm remains: 24 − 6 = 18. Take away 4, then 2. Each task begins with the original table lengths.

answers.label: Reading · 1
answers.text: Little first guessed the note was hiding inside. The key and action moved a hammer, which struck strings. The vibrating strings and soundboard made the sound as they moved.

answers.label: Reading · 2
answers.text: The bridge carries a string's vibration into the soundboard. The broad soundboard vibrates and moves air, which carries sound to our ears.

answers.label: Writing
answers.text: Accept a scene-based drawing, dictation, or 1–3 sentences. For example: The hammer taps a string and comes away. The string keeps vibrating. For pitch comparisons, keep the other string conditions the same.

parentGuidance: Wonder first; explanations can wait. This is an acoustic piano; digital pianos usually make sound electronically through speakers. Museum models omit parts and exaggerate motion. They are not building plans or exact key/string counts. The action lets the hammer rebound while a key stays down. The bridge carries string vibration into the soundboard, which moves more air using energy from the strike. Pitch depends on vibration rate; loudness depends largely on vibration size. Compare string lengths with material, thickness, and tension unchanged: longer gives lower pitch; shorter gives higher. For the same string and vibrating length, tighter gives higher and looser gives lower. Real pianos combine length, thickness, and tension; low strings are longer and heavier. Pressing harder mainly changes loudness. Many notes use two or three strings. With the sustain pedal up, dampers return as keys are released; the highest strings often lack dampers. The story uses a middle key. Add the missing bridge or air to Little's sketch. Pictures, gentle humming, talking, and drawing are enough. Do not open a piano, touch or tighten strings, or build these models. Welcome dictation and stop whenever you have had enough.
